title: School Culture Begins with Teacher Identity: Why Scholarly Identity Matters for Everyone
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes extends Doug Lemov's concept of 'scholarly identity' - typically applied to students - to teachers, arguing professional identity develops 'from the outside in' through repeated experiences of success, exactly as pupils develop scholarly identity through classroom success. Drawing on Beijaard, Meijer and Verloop's account of dynamic professional identity and Kelchtermans's concept of 'teacher tension' (competing demands like nurturing-yet-accountable, creative-yet-evidence-based), she argues strong school culture reduces cognitive load by making expectations shared rather than individually negotiated each day. Applying Lemov's 'warm/strict' teacher framework to adults, she argues the strongest professional cultures combine genuine care with uncompromising expectations, reframing coaching feedback from 'you need my help because you're failing' to 'I'm investing in you because your development matters.' She closes by arguing identity, not implementation fidelity, is the real curriculum of school culture.
points: Hughes's central move - applying Lemov's 'scholarly identity' concept (built for students) directly to teachers - offers a genuinely novel reframe of how professional culture shapes staff behaviour.

She uses Kelchtermans's concept of 'teacher tension' (competing demands like nurturing-yet-accountable) to argue coherent school culture reduces cognitive load by pre-resolving daily professional dilemmas.

Her reframed coaching language - shifting from 'you need my help because you're failing' to 'I'm investing in you because your development matters' - is a concrete, transferable script for leaders giving feedback.
Her closing claim that 'identity is the real curriculum of culture' repositions school improvement work as fundamentally about who people believe they are, not just what systems are in place.
quotes: Just as students become scholars by repeatedly experiencing themselves as scholars, teachers become expert professionals by repeatedly experiencing themselves as successful professionals.

Kelchtermans argues that teaching is characterised by continual vulnerability because professional identity is constantly exposed to judgement from students, colleagues, leaders, parents and inspection systems. These tensions are not signs of weak teachers. They are structural features of the profession.
In high-functioning schools, expectations become shared rather than individually negotiated. Teachers no longer have to decide hundreds of times each day what good behaviour looks like.

The most effective schools I have seen create environments where professional feedback communicates confidence rather than criticism: I am coaching you because I believe you are capable of exceptional teaching.

When leaders consistently reinforce trust, competence and shared purpose, teachers begin to see themselves differently. When teachers consistently reinforce trust, competence and scholarly habits, students begin to see themselves differently.
